chapter: Chicago, the Marable boats and Marge's St. Louis family band
title: Charlie Creath's death in 1951
summary: On the way to Europe in 1951 they visited Charlie, then got a telegram on the boat saying he was dead. In Paris his wife wrote that he killed himself over a bookmaking debt.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: How long did he -- what happened to him?
Well, when we were on our way to Europe we stopped to see him. We spent a whole night with him and it looked like he didn't want us to go out no place. So we
spent our time with him and when we got on the boat we received a telegram and they said Charlie was dead and everything. But we didn't know how.
And this would be when, Zutty?
This was 1951.
'51, yeah. How old would he be?
Well, Charlie -- oh, let's see. Well, never mind.
But what had he done in the meantime between that time when he died and when you --

Well, he had a bookie, see. That was causing the death, I think, because he had a bookie, Lodo and he, they were good pals, and they were running this bookie race horses, you know, and everything like that. And so Charlie were waiting for Lodo to come in and pay off a debt, like he was threatened or something, you know, to pay this debt off see. But Lodo didn't get in, so Charlie waited on him and waited on him and everything, and he never did show up with this bread.
Yeah.
So right after that, that's when Charlie committed suicide.
Oh.
Yeah, he committed suicide. Drank lysol and shot himself.
Oh it was the thought of the debt
that was worrying him. The debt, the fact that he couldn't pay off.
Yeah, that's right.
Oh, that's a shame.
That's what we always put it to. Because we received this telegram on the boat and said Charlie had died. But we didn't know about why and how until we got to Paris.
Right.
And that's when Charlie's wife wrote us a letter and explained everything.
